title: King Grisly-Beard
paragraphs: Far off in the East, a great king had a daughter of striking beauty. But she was so proud, so arrogant and so full of herself that not one of the princes who came courting was good enough for her, and she simply mocked them all.

One day the king gave a great feast and invited all her suitors. They sat in a row, arranged by rank: kings, princes, dukes, earls, counts, barons and knights. Then the princess came in, and as she passed along the row she had a spiteful remark for every one of them. The first was too fat. “He’s as round as a tub,” she said. The next was too tall. “What a maypole!” she said. The next was too short. “What a dumpling!” she said. The fourth was too pale, and she called him “Wallface.” The fifth was too red, so she called him “Coxcomb.” The sixth was not quite straight, so she said he was like a green stick that had been left to dry above a baker’s oven. And so she had a joke to crack about every one of them. But she laughed more than anyone at a good king who was there. “Look at him,” she said. “His beard is like an old mop. I’ll call him Grisly-beard.” And so the king got the nickname Grisly-beard.

But the old king was very angry when he saw how his daughter behaved and how she mistreated all his guests. He vowed that, whether she liked it or not, she would marry the first man to come to the door, be he prince or beggar.

Two days later a traveling fiddler came by and began to play under the window and beg for coins. When the king heard him, he said, “Let him come in.” They brought in a dirty-looking fellow, and when he had sung before the king and the princess, he asked for a reward. The king said, “You have sung so well that I will give you my daughter as your wife.” The princess begged and pleaded, but the king said, “I swore to give you to the first man who came, and I will keep my word.” Words and tears were no use. The parson was sent for, and she was married to the fiddler. When that was done, the king said, “Now get ready to leave. You can’t stay here. You must travel on with your husband.”

Then the fiddler set off and took her with him, and soon they came to a great forest. “Tell me,” she said, “whose forest is this?” “It belongs to King Grisly-beard,” he answered. “If you had taken him, it would all have been yours.” “Oh, what an unlucky wretch I am!” she sighed. “If only I had married King Grisly-beard!” Next they came to some fine meadows. “Whose are these beautiful green meadows?” she asked. “They belong to King Grisly-beard. If you had taken him, they would all have been yours.” “Oh, what an unlucky wretch I am!” she said. “If only I had married King Grisly-beard!”

Next they reached a great city. “Whose splendid city is this?” she asked. “It belongs to King Grisly-beard,” he said. “If you had taken him, it would all be yours now.” “Oh, what a wretch I am!” she sighed. “Why didn’t I marry King Grisly-beard?” “That’s no concern of mine,” said the fiddler. “Why should you want another husband? Am I not good enough for you?”

Finally they came to a tiny cottage. “What a miserable place!” she said. “Who owns this filthy little hole?” The fiddler answered, “It’s yours and mine. This is where we’ll live.” “Where are your servants?” she cried. “What would we do with servants?” he said. “You’ll do whatever needs doing yourself. Now light the fire, put the water on, and cook my supper. I’m very tired.” But the princess knew nothing about lighting fires or cooking, and the fiddler had to help her. After a very meager meal they went to bed, and early the next morning he woke her to clean the house. They lived like this for two days. When everything in the cottage had been eaten, the man said, “Wife, we can’t carry on like this, spending money and earning none. You must learn to weave baskets.” He went out, cut some willow branches, and brought them home. She began to weave, but it hurt her fingers badly. “I can see this work is no good,” he said. “Try spinning instead. Maybe you’ll be better at that.” So she sat down and tried to spin, but the thread cut her soft fingers until they bled. “Look at that,” said the fiddler. “You’re good for nothing. You can’t do any work at all. What a bargain I’ve made! Well, I’ll try setting up a business in pots and pans, and you can stand in the market and sell them.” “Oh no,” she sighed. “If anyone from my father’s court walks past and sees me standing in the market, how they’ll laugh at me!”

Her husband didn’t care about that. He said she had to work unless she wanted to starve. At first the business went well, because many people saw such a beautiful woman and bought her wares, paying without even thinking of taking the goods away. They lived off this as long as it lasted. Then her husband bought a new stock of pottery, and she settled down with it in a corner of the market. But soon a drunken soldier came along on his horse, rode straight into her stall, and smashed everything into a thousand pieces. She began to cry and had no idea what to do. “Oh, what will become of me?” she said. “What will my husband say?” She ran home and told him everything. “Who would ever have thought you could be so foolish,” he said, “as to set up a pottery stall in the corner of the market, where everybody walks by? But enough crying. I can see you’re not fit for this kind of work, so I went to the king’s palace and asked whether they needed a kitchen maid. They say they’ll take you, and there you’ll get plenty to eat.”
So the princess became a kitchen maid and helped the cook with all the dirtiest jobs. She was allowed to take home some of the leftover meat, and that was what they lived on.

She hadn’t been there long when she heard that the king’s eldest son was riding past on his way to be married. She went to one of the windows and looked out. Everything was ready, and all the splendor and glitter of the court was on display. She grieved bitterly then over the pride and foolishness that had brought her so low. The servants gave her some of the rich food, and she put it in her basket to take home.

Suddenly, just as she was leaving, the king’s son walked in, dressed in gold. When he saw a beautiful woman at the door, he took her by the hand and said she must dance with him. She shook with fear, because she saw that it was King Grisly-beard, who was making fun of her. But he held on tight and led her inside, and the lid of the basket came off, so that the food spilled all over the floor. Everyone laughed and jeered at her, and she was so ashamed that she wished she were a thousand feet underground. She dashed for the door to run away, but King Grisly-beard caught her on the steps and brought her back. “Don’t be afraid of me,” he said. “I am the fiddler who lived with you in the hut. I took you there because I truly loved you. I am also the soldier who overturned your stall. I did all of this only to cure you of your silly pride, and to show you how foolishly you had treated me. Now it’s all over. You have learned wisdom, and it’s time to hold our wedding feast.”

Then the chamberlains came and brought her the most beautiful dresses. Her father and his whole court had already arrived and welcomed her home to her wedding. There was joy on every face and in every heart. The feast was magnificent. They danced and sang, everyone was merry, and I only wish that you and I had been there too.
